name: Umar Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so please tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Umar, 58, and I operate a haul truck at a big mine. I came to this work late, so I'm still one of the junior drivers; I check the tyres and the bed before the morning queue, then carry rock from the pit to the crusher. I like getting a loaded truck round the north ramp cleanly, but the long climb into the cab is hard on my knees, and I still ask the quicker drivers to show me things. I finished secondary school, and most evenings I use an AI quiz on my phone to go over the safety manual before bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the machines still need someone in the cab at six in the morning. The office may save a few minutes on forms, but the road up to the pit is still rough and wet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm more worried about my own place on the shift than about an AI miracle. I'm 58 and still junior because I came into mining late, and the newer operators can clear a loading lane faster than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking my scheduled truck shifts and ask supervisor Marta to watch my reversing on the north ramp this month. I already use an AI app each evening to quiz myself on the safety manual, and I'll keep doing that; if the small changes arrive, I'll check my roster in their first year before changing course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly steady about the technology and a little embarrassed about being the older learner. A missed shift would bite because our savings cover only about four months of bills, but I don't expect the AI itself to take the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the four months of savings feel enough or insufficient?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son and daughter are grown and paying their own rent now. My partner Leila and I still cover our own flat, groceries and her bus fare, so four months saved isn't a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your supervisor about your place on the shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd ask Marta is whether my driving is improving enough to keep a full roster. I don't want a polite compliment; I want to know what I do wrong on that bend when the gravel is loose.

say: I would tell the **crew** that the truck still needs a driver on the rough pit road.
I would say the **office forms** may get quicker while our shifts look much the same.
think: I worry more about my **junior standing** than the small AI change.
My **four months** of savings cannot carry my partner and me into retirement.
do: Keep driving my **scheduled shifts** and ask Marta to assess my reversing this month.
Continue the **safety quiz** each evening and check my roster after the small changes arrive.
feel: I feel **steady** about AI but embarrassed to be an older learner.
S0.quote: I'm 58 and still junior because I came into mining late, and the newer operators can clear a loading lane faster than me.
fieldNote: His **age** matters mainly because he entered mining late and is still learning a task younger operators perform more smoothly.
The **four-month cushion** helps with a short disruption, yet he is already watching every shift because his household needs his pay.

steps.text: Drive scheduled truck shifts and ask Marta to assess north-ramp reversing
Use the AI app for an evening safety-manual quiz

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should train drivers before it trims the roster, and the union ought to see the numbers. Our dispatch sheets and route plans could change quickly, even if a person still has to steer a loaded truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see the office cutting a dispatcher and pushing more decisions onto a screen in my cab. I might gain a little from the route software, but a junior driver is an easy name to leave off overtime, and overtime helps us keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd ask our union representative for the written plan on driver training and rosters, and I'd attend the next branch meeting. I'd also ask Marta for a turn with the new route display and practise it on the empty loop; during the first year of the change, I'd set aside the overtime I still get instead of treating it as spending money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm curious about the screen and uneasy about the hours. There is time to learn, but a shrinking roster could swallow that time faster than I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you recall a planning change that affected a shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter the office changed the loading order without telling us until breakfast. Three trucks waited while the loader moved across the pit, which is why I want a person from the cab in any planning meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would you want the union to ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the union to ask who gets the training on paid time and whether older junior drivers get a fair turn. A poster about opportunity means little if I have to learn the display after a twelve-hour shift.

say: I would call for **paid training** before the company cuts a driver roster.
I would ask the **union** to see the figures behind any changed shifts.
think: I think automated **dispatch** could reduce office jobs and overtime before trucks drive themselves.
My junior place makes lost **overtime** a realistic blow to our savings.
do: Ask the **union representative** for the roster plan and attend the next branch meeting.
Practise the **route display** on the empty loop and bank overtime during the first year.
feel: I feel **curious** about the screen and uneasy about losing hours.
S1.quote: A poster about opportunity means little if I have to learn the display after a twelve-hour shift.
fieldNote: He separates the **dispatch screen** from the truck itself, expecting hours and office work to change before cab work does.
His request for **paid training** reflects both his political views and the difficulty of learning after a long shift.

steps.text: Attend the next union branch meeting about training and rosters
Practise the new route display on the empty loop
Bank overtime pay during the first year of changed dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 thinking AI isn't a robot at the wheel, but 2031 might be. I'd ask the company and union to sit down now about paid retraining and how many cab jobs will remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60 when the thinking system arrives, I could still be driving while it plans every trip and writes every report. At 63 when capable robots arrive, I don't trust my junior place to survive; four months of savings would not cover the years before I can afford to stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training office this month whether I can take the paid vehicle-maintenance course, and I'd enroll if the place and wages are guaranteed. I'd keep driving and put every overtime payment into savings; in 2029 I'd also apply for maintenance-assistant openings at the two nearby mines rather than wait for a robot demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one scares me badly, though I'm not frozen. I can learn a workshop job, but I can't make a three-year clock longer, and Leila can't pay our bills alone on her part-time library wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the maintenance course still protect you after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know whether the company would keep enough mechanics once the robots can repair things too. I'd take the course for an option, not because a certificate is a shield against the same technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change at home first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leila and I would cancel the short coast trip we planned for spring. The children have their own homes and would listen, but I wouldn't ask them to carry our rent when they have their own bills.

say: I would tell the **crew** that thinking AI could plan trips in 2028, with capable robots around 2031.
I would demand **paid retraining** talks between the company and union now.
think: I expect my **junior cab job** to be at serious risk when robots arrive at 63.
Our **four-month cushion** cannot fund the remaining years of work I may need.
do: Seek a **paid maintenance course** now and enroll if wages and a place are guaranteed.
Bank **overtime** and apply to nearby maintenance-assistant openings in 2029.
feel: I feel **scared**, but I still have a short list of moves to make.
S2.quote: At 63 when capable robots arrive, I don't trust my junior place to survive; four months of savings would not cover the years before I can afford to stop working.
fieldNote: He expects **thinking AI** to take planning and reports in 2028, then sees the truck role itself threatened around 2031.
His proposed **maintenance course** is a wager on time, and he admits robots may eventually threaten workshop work as well.

steps.text: Enroll in the vehicle-maintenance course if the place and wages are guaranteed
Put every overtime payment into savings
Apply for maintenance-assistant openings at two nearby mines in 2029
Cancel the planned spring coast trip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the company time to publish a real plan, with drivers at the table. Thinking AI in 2031 could replace our scheduling and paperwork, and capable robots around 2034 could take the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 when the thinking work goes and 66 when the trucks can work without us. I might be ready to leave by 66, but I won't pretend retirement is paid for just because the date looks close on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Leila to go through our monthly bills with me this weekend and set a savings target we can actually keep. I'd stay on the truck while I improve my driving, and I'd take a paid maintenance course if offered; in 2032 I'd check the new job notices every month and apply for a workshop opening if the roster starts thinning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels like room to breathe, with a knot still in it. I want to make a choice about leaving mining, not be told on a Friday that my last shift was Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where could the extra savings come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat costs us more than either child now costs us, because they support themselves. If we stopped buying takeaway meals after late shifts, we could probably save a modest sum each month without pretending that Leila's library pay will replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of company promise would change your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for a written date on each equipment trial and a funded training place before it changes driver numbers. A promise to retrain everyone is too loose when I'm junior and the workshop has only a few benches.

say: I would ask for a **written plan** with drivers at the table over the five-year warning.
I would explain that **planning work** changes in 2031 and cab work faces robots around 2034.
think: At **66**, I may want to leave, but my retirement income is not settled.
I need the extra years to build **savings**, not simply watch the technology arrive.
do: Set a **monthly savings target** with Leila and stay on the truck while improving my driving.
Take a **paid course** if offered, then check workshop openings monthly in 2032.
feel: I feel **relieved** by the time and uneasy about the final decision.
S3.quote: I might be ready to leave by 66, but I won't pretend retirement is paid for just because the date looks close on paper.
fieldNote: He treats **2034** as a possible exit age, but refuses to count retirement income he has not established.
His **monthly budget** is practical because the grown children support themselves; the flat and his wages are the household stakes.

steps.text: Set a monthly savings target with Leila and reduce takeaway meals
Keep driving truck shifts while improving reversing on the north ramp
Take a paid maintenance course if the mine offers one
Apply for a workshop opening in 2032 if the driver roster thins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger drivers ten years is enough time to demand useful training, not an excuse for management to wait. Thinking AI could do the schedules in 2036, and the hands-on robot date would be around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 at the first date and 71 when the capable robots reach the cab. I hope to have stopped full-time shifts before 71, but I cannot call myself safe until Leila and I have worked out what income we'd actually live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd book an appointment with the union's retirement adviser and bring our savings figures, then I'd keep working the truck while my health and roster allow. I'd keep the AI safety quizzes and, in 2037, review the numbers with Leila again; if we can cover our bills, I'd bring retirement forward before the robot years, and if we can't, I'd keep applying for paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more hopeful with a decade, but not carefree. My knees tell me ten more years of climbing the truck steps isn't guaranteed either, even if the mine still wants drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes retirement uncertain even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I once thought turning 65 would settle the question, but our rent and savings have never obeyed a birthday. The adviser can show us the figures; until then, retirement is a possibility, not a cheque in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What else should a company ask an older learner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The other question is whether the company will let an older junior driver keep learning safely. I use the AI quiz because I hate guessing at a warning sign, and I would want the training time on my shift rather than after it.

say: I would tell younger drivers the **ten-year warning** should buy real training and bargaining time.
I would explain that **thinking AI** arrives in 2036 and capable robots around 2039.
think: I hope to stop full-time shifts before **71**, but our retirement income needs checking.
My **knees** may limit truck work before any robot does.
do: Book the union **retirement adviser** now and bring our savings figures.
Keep paid **truck shifts** and AI safety quizzes, then review the budget with Leila in 2037.
feel: I feel **hopeful** about the time, with real concern for my health and income.
S4.quote: My knees tell me ten more years of climbing the truck steps isn't guaranteed either, even if the mine still wants drivers.
fieldNote: The **decade** moves the risk from immediate displacement toward the unresolved cost and timing of retirement.
He keeps **paid work** central and considers early retirement only if an adviser and household budget show the bills can be covered.

steps.text: Book the union retirement adviser and bring household savings figures
Keep driving paid truck shifts while health and roster allow
Bring retirement forward if the 2037 budget covers household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because I would be 63 when robots could do the driving and I have only about four months of bills saved. I'd need paid training while the truck work still exists, a fair shot at nearby workshop jobs, and a written roster plan the union can challenge. I would still work and apply for those jobs; I cannot retire on a date alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether someone who's 58 and still learning gets the same training as a young driver. The company puts a hand on my shoulder and says I'm doing fine, but I need time in the cab and honest feedback on the ramp. My age doesn't stop me learning; an unpaid course after a long shift might.

headlineQuote: My age doesn't stop me learning; an unpaid course after a long shift might.
portrait: Umar is a **58-year-old junior** haul-truck driver who entered mining late and practises safety rules with an AI app.
His grown children support themselves, while he and Leila live on **four months** of savings and their current wages.
He sees **dispatch** changing before driving, then expects capable robots to threaten his cab job after each AGI date.
He asks for **paid training**, keeps working, and checks retirement against actual household bills rather than age alone.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove his cab work around age 63, before his short savings cushion can support retirement.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid training**, fair access to nearby workshop jobs, and a written roster plan the union can challenge.
